📝 Note 1 (Bilateral Disc Swelling: Clinical Emergency & Diagnostic Framework - 17/02/2026):
Clinical Signs of True Swelling

Blurring of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer
Obscuration of major retinal vessels as they leave the disc
Paton’s lines (circumferential retinal folds)
Flame-shaped hemorrhages at or near the disc margin
Cotton wool spots (indicative of axonal ischemia)
Absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsation (SVP)
Hyperemic appearance of the optic nerve head

📝 Note 2 (NEOVASCULAR GLAUCOMA (NVG): A Comprehensive Guide - 14/02/2026):
Key Causes & Risk Factors

Ischaemic CrVO (common); risk of progression to NVG is 50%.
Diabetic retinopathy (common); risk of NVG highest in PDr.
Other vascular disorders: OIS, CrAO, BrVO.
Other retinal disease: chronic retinal detachment, sickle cell retinopathy.
Retinal or choroidal tumours.

📝 Note 3 (SEVENTH NERVE DISORDERS: THE OPHTHALMIC PERSPECTIVE - 14/02/2026):
Differential: Isolated vs Complex?

1. Check for involvement of all other cranial nerves.
2. Check Vn (cerebellopontine lesions).
3. Check VIn (lesion in pons).
4. Check VIIn (cerebellopontine angle lesions).
5. Check for alteration of taste.
6. Check for alteration of salivation.
7. Check for alteration of lacrimation.

📝 Note 4 (Uveal Emergencies: VKH Disease & Sympathetic Ophthalmia - 14/02/2026):
Management of VKH

Step 1: Liaise with physician.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g. 1–2mg/kg/d prednisolone PO or IVMP 1g/d for 3d).
Step 3: For resistant or recurrent disease, add corticosteroid-sparing agents (immunosuppressants).
Immunosuppressants include: Methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus, and ciclosporin.
